_about: Interactive learning activities. Every fact here is from the sources listed in docs/CREDITS.md (section 'Five-day mission facts'). Game numbers elsewhere are simplified; these facts are real.

selection.title: WHO GETS TO BE AN ASTRONAUT?
selection.intro: Commander Okafor hands you a stack of cards. Some are real NASA astronaut requirements. Some are myths. Sort them.

items.text: You must be a U.S. citizen (dual citizens can apply).
items.explain: Real. NASA's astronaut candidate program is open to U.S. citizens, including dual citizens. Other countries select astronauts through their own agencies, like the CSA or ESA.

items.text: You need a master's degree in a STEM field, or an equivalent such as a medical degree or test pilot school.
items.explain: Real. Engineering, biology, physics, computer science or math all count. Two years of doctoral study, an M.D. or a test pilot school program can stand in for the master's.

items.text: You must already be a jet pilot.
items.explain: Myth. No previous flight experience is required. Many astronauts are scientists, doctors and engineers who learn to fly the T-38 jet during training.

items.text: You must be younger than 35.
items.explain: Myth! NASA has no age limit. John Glenn flew on the Space Shuttle in 1998 when he was 77.

items.text: You must pass NASA's long-duration spaceflight physical exam.
items.explain: Real. Candidates must be able to pass the long-duration flight physical. Vision only needs to be correctable to 20/20, so glasses are fine.

items.text: You need years of professional work in your field after your degree (or many hours flying jets).
items.explain: Real. NASA asks for related professional experience after the degree, or at least 1,000 hours as pilot-in-command of jet aircraft. Teaching STEM counts too.

selection.outro: Thousands apply and only about ten are picked per class. Then comes about two years of training. Rivera will show you some of it.

training.title: ASTRONAUT CANDIDATE TRAINING
training.intro: Astronaut candidates train for about two years before they can be assigned to a mission. Match each kind of training to what it's for.

items.text: Why do candidates practice spacewalks underwater in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory?
options: Floating in water feels a lot like weightlessness
To learn to swim to the Moon
items.explain: Weighted to float in place, a suited astronaut moves much like in microgravity. NASA's pool holds 6.2 million gallons and a full-size model of the space station.

items.text: Why does every candidate fly the T-38 supersonic jet, even non-pilots?
options: To practice fast decisions in a demanding, unforgiving environment
Because the rocket is shaped like a T-38
items.explain: Flying a jet trains teamwork and quick decisions under pressure, skills that carry over to spaceflight.

items.text: What is survival training for?
options: Staying safe if a capsule lands somewhere remote, on land or water
items.explain: Candidates train in land and water survival in case a spacecraft comes down far from the recovery teams. It also builds trust inside the crew.

items.text: Why do Artemis-era candidates study geology in the field?
options: To pick the most useful rock samples on the Moon
items.explain: Moonwalkers act as field geologists. Choosing the right samples helps scientists on Earth learn how the Moon formed and where water ice is.

training.outro: Robotics is on the list too: candidates learn to fly the station's Canadarm2 robotic arm, which you just practiced.

health.title: CREW HEALTH CHECK
health.intro: Rivera points at the exercise bike. 'Before you ride, predict what low gravity does to a body.'

items.text: In weightlessness, without exercise, about how much bone density can a weight-bearing bone lose each MONTH?
items.explain: Around 1 to 1.5 percent per month. Bones reshape themselves when gravity stops loading them, a bit like osteoporosis on Earth.

items.text: How much exercise do space station crews do to fight this?
items.explain: About two hours a day on a treadmill, a bike and a weightlifting machine called ARED. Even then some bone is lost.

items.text: The Moon has one-sixth of Earth's gravity. Will the crew still need daily exercise here?
options: Yes, one-sixth of Earth's gravity loads the body much less
items.explain: Scientists still don't know exactly how much partial gravity protects bones and muscles, so lunar crews plan to keep exercising. That's why this bike is here.

health.outro: Health check logged. Keep riding: strong legs make the walk to the shelter faster.

plant.title: PLANT THE GREENHOUSE
plant.intro: Dr. Tanaka hands you a tray of seed pillows. 'Our garden is modelled on NASA's Veggie growth unit. Let's set it up.'

items.text: There's no garden soil on the Moon. What holds the seeds and roots?
options: Plant pillows: small bags of growing material, fertilizer and seeds
items.explain: Veggie uses rooting 'pillows'. They hold the seeds, a clay-based growing material and slow-release fertilizer.

items.text: How do the pillows get water without it floating off or flooding the roots?
options: Water wicks up into the pillows from a reservoir
The crew pours a cup on top
items.explain: A wick draws water slowly from a reservoir into the pillows, so the roots get water and air.

items.text: Which crop did NASA astronauts first grow and eat on the space station?
items.explain: It was picked because it's easy to grow, nutritious and tasty. Our first beds are red romaine too.

plant.outro: Seeds planted. Tomorrow we test which light recipe grows them best.

light_test.title: LIGHT-RECIPE EXPERIMENT
light_test.intro: Three test trays, three LED light recipes, same seeds. Make a prediction, then watch 30 days of growth in 10 seconds.

items.text: Which tray will grow the LEAST?
items.explain: Leaves look green because they reflect most green light, so green alone feeds a plant poorly. Red and blue are the colors plants use most.

items.text: Veggie uses red, blue AND some green LEDs. Why add the green?
options: Green makes plants grow twice as fast
So the plants look normal and the crew can spot sick leaves
items.explain: Under only red and blue, plants look purple-pink. A little green makes them look like food again, so the crew can check their health by eye.

light_test.outro: Result logged to science: red + blue does the growing; green helps people see. Our model numbers are simplified, but the idea is the real one NASA used.

regolith.title: SOIL OR REGOLITH?
regolith.intro: Tanaka slides two jars across the bench: Earth garden soil and lunar regolith. Sort each fact to the right jar.

items.text: Full of rotting leaves, worms and microbes that feed plants.
items.explain: Living soil is rich in organic matter. The Moon has none of that.

items.text: Sharp, glassy grains made by billions of years of meteorite impacts.
items.explain: Regolith is crushed rock and glass. It's jagged, clings to everything and has no organic matter.

items.text: In a 2022 study, seeds sprouted in samples of it, but the plants grew small and stressed.
items.explain: University of Florida scientists grew small mustard-family plants in Apollo samples. Everything sprouted, but roots and leaves grew stunted.

items.text: Holds water and air in tiny spaces that roots can use.
items.explain: Good soil is crumbly. That's why lunar farms will probably use pillows, hydroponics, or regolith treated with fertilizer and microbes.

regolith.outro: That's why our greenhouse grows in pillows and water, not raw Moon dust. Regolith is still useful: piled on a roof, it makes great radiation shielding.

harvest.title: FIRST HARVEST
harvest.intro: The first leaves are ready. Tanaka cleans them with a food-safe wipe. Before you taste, a little history.

items.text: When did NASA astronauts first eat lettuce they grew in space?
items.explain: Scott Kelly, Kjell Lindgren and Kimiya Yui tasted 'Outredgeous' red romaine from Veggie. Kelly said it tasted kind of like arugula.

items.text: Besides vitamins, why does fresh food matter on a long mission?
options: Caring for plants and eating fresh food can lift the crew's mood
items.explain: Fresh food adds nutrients that fade in stored meals, and having something green to look after helps people far from home.

harvest.outro: Crunchy. Science points logged. The crops will keep growing if the grow lights stay on.

weather.title: SPACE WEATHER WATCH
weather.intro: The comms desk shows a DONKI-style feed: NASA's database of solar flares, eruptions and particle storms seen near Earth. Sort each event.
bins: Can warn of a particle storm

items.text: A big solar flare flashes near the middle of the Sun.
items.explain: Big flares often come with eruptions that can launch fast particles our way.

items.text: A fast coronal mass ejection (CME) is racing away from the Sun.
items.explain: A fast CME drives a shock wave that can speed particles up to nearly the speed of light. Forecasters watch these closely.

items.text: The outpost moves into the shadow of a ridge.
items.explain: Shadow drains the battery, but it has nothing to do with solar particles.

items.text: It's a full moon as seen from Earth.
items.explain: Moon phases are just sunlight and geometry. They don't affect radiation.

weather.outro: Tomorrow we drill the shelter. When the alarm goes, you'll know exactly where to run.
